lessons.title: Determining Optimal Planting Dates
lessons.body: In Africa, potato planting dates depend on rainfall, temperature, and altitude. Potatoes grow best when soil temperature is between 15Â°C and 20Â°C. If you plant when it's too hot (above 30Â°C), tubers may not form. If too cold (below 10Â°C), growth stops. In highland areas like Kenya's Nyandarua or Ethiopia's Holeta, the main planting season is when the long rains beginâusually March to April. A second season can be planted in September to October with short rains. In lowland areas with irrigation, you can plant year-round, but avoid the hottest months. For rain-fed farming, plant 2-3 weeks after the first consistent rains, when soil is moist but not waterlogged. Waterlogged soil causes seed pieces to rot. A simple test: squeeze a handful of soilâif it holds together but breaks apart when you poke it, it's ready. If it drips water, wait. Also consider frost: potatoes are sensitive to frost. In areas like the South African Highveld, plant after the last frost. In West Africa's Jos Plateau, plant at the start of the rainy season (April-May). To be sure, ask local extension officers or experienced farmers for the best planting window in your area. Keep a farm diary: note planting date, rainfall, and yield. After 2-3 seasons, you'll know your optimal dates. Planting at the right time can increase yields by 30-50%. Don't guessâuse a simple rain gauge and soil thermometer. These cost little and save your crop.

lessons.title: Planting Depth and Spacing Guidelines
lessons.body: Plant seed potatoes at a depth of 8-10 cm from the top of the seed piece to the soil surface. If you plant too shallow (less than 5 cm), tubers may turn green (sunburn) and become bitter. If too deep (more than 15 cm), sprouts take longer to emerge and may rot. In sandy soils, plant deeper (10-12 cm) because soil dries out faster. In clay soils, plant shallower (6-8 cm) to avoid waterlogging. Spacing: for large seed pieces (whole small tubers or cut pieces with 2-3 eyes), space plants 25-30 cm apart within the row. For smaller seed pieces, 20-25 cm. Between rows, keep 70-90 cm apart. This allows air movement, reduces disease, and makes hilling easier. If you plant too close, you get many small tubers; too far, you waste land. A common mistake is planting in a grid. Instead, use ridges or furrows. In Africa, many farmers use the

method: cut large tubers into pieces with at least two eyes, then plant. But cutting increases rot riskâif you cut, let pieces dry for 1-2 days in shade before planting. For whole small tubers (30-40 g), plant directly. A hectare needs about 2,000-2,500 kg of seed potatoes if spaced 30x75 cm. That's roughly 20-25 bags of 100 kg each. Always plant with the cut side down or the eyes facing up. Cover with soil and press gently. Mark rows with sticks or string to keep spacing even. After planting, the soil should be level or slightly mounded. Don't leave seed pieces exposedâbirds and rodents will eat them.

lessons.title: Mechanical vs. Manual Planting Methods
lessons.body: Manual planting is the most common method in Africa. It uses hand hoes, machetes, or dibbers (pointed sticks). Steps: clear the field, dig a furrow 10 cm deep with a hoe, place seed pieces 25-30 cm apart, cover with soil. A person can plant about 0.2-0.3 hectares per day. Manual planting is cheap, but slow and labor-intensive. It's good for small plots (less than 1 hectare) and steep slopes where machines can't go. Mechanical planting uses tractor-drawn planters. These machines open a furrow, drop seed pieces at correct spacing, and cover them in one pass. A two-row planter can plant 1-2 hectares per day. But they are expensive to buy or hire (US$50-100 per hectare). They also require well-prepared, stone-free soil. In Africa, mechanical planting is used on large commercial farms in South Africa, Kenya, and Egypt. For smallholders, a middle option is a hand-pushed planter (e.g., a jab planter). It's faster than a hoe and costs less than a tractor. If you use a mechanical planter, calibrate it first: check spacing and depth on a small area. Also, ensure seed pieces are uniform in sizeâotherwise, the machine may clog. For manual planting, organize labor into teams: one person digs, one drops, one covers. This speeds up work. Whichever method, plant in straight rows to allow later hilling and spraying. After planting, clean the tools to prevent disease spread. If you hire a tractor, book earlyâeveryone plants at the same time.

lessons.title: Hilling and Ridging After Planting
lessons.body: Hilling (also called ridging or earthing up) means pulling soil around the base of potato plants. Do it when plants are 15-20 cm tallâabout 3-4 weeks after planting. Hilling covers the stems, encouraging more tubers to form and preventing them from turning green. It also improves drainage and weed control. Use a hoe or a tractor-drawn ridger. For manual hilling, work along each row: pull soil from between rows to form a ridge 15-20 cm high around the plants. Be careful not to bury the leaves completelyâleave the top 10 cm of the plant exposed. In Africa, many farmers hill twice: first when plants are 15 cm, second 2-3 weeks later. This is especially important in areas with heavy rain, as it prevents waterlogging. If you plant in flat beds, hilling is a must. If you already planted on ridges, you may only need to repair them. Hilling also helps control weedsâbury small weeds. But don't hill when soil is too wet; it compacts the soil and spreads disease. Wait until soil crumbles. For large farms, a tractor with a disc ridger can hill 1 hectare in 1-2 hours. For small farms, a team of 5 people can hill 0.5 hectare in a day. After hilling, the field should look like a series of parallel ridges. This also makes harvesting easierâyou can dig along the ridges. If you see potato tubers pushing out of the soil, hill immediately. Exposed tubers turn green and are unsellable. Hilling is one of the simplest ways to increase yield by 10-20%.

lessons.title: Use of Pre-Emergence Herbicides
lessons.body: Pre-emergence herbicides kill weeds before they sprout. Apply them right after planting, before potato plants emerge. They work by forming a chemical barrier in the top 2-5 cm of soil. Common products for potatoes include metribuzin (e.g., Sencor), pendimethalin (e.g., Prowl), and linuron. In Africa, metribuzin is widely available. Use the correct dose: for metribuzin 70% WP, apply 0.5-1.0 kg per hectare in 200-400 liters of water. For pendimethalin 33% EC, use 3-4 liters per hectare. Always read the labelâoverdosing harms potatoes. Apply with a knapsack sprayer or tractor sprayer. Calibrate your sprayer first: spray water on a 10 m x 10 m area, measure how much water you used, then adjust. Spray evenly over the soil surface. Do not spray if rain is expected within 6 hoursârain washes the herbicide away. Also, do not spray on wet soil or when it's windy. After spraying, avoid disturbing the soilâhilling later will break the barrier. That's why many farmers apply pre-emergence herbicides after the final hilling, but before potatoes emerge. If weeds already emerged, pre-emergence herbicides won't work. You must hand-weed first. Pre-emergence herbicides save labor: one spray can replace 2-3 hand-weedings. But they can damage potatoes if used incorrectly. Never use a herbicide not labeled for potatoes. Also, rotate herbicides to prevent resistant weeds. For organic farmers, use mulch (e.g., dry grass) instead. Always wear protective clothing: gloves, mask, and long sleeves. Store herbicides away from food and children.

lessons.title: Irrigation Setup for Newly Planted Potatoes
lessons.body: Newly planted potatoes need consistent moisture, but not waterlogging. For the first 2 weeks after planting, keep soil moist but not soaked. If you have irrigation, apply 20-25 mm of water per week. In sandy soil, water more often (every 3-4 days). In clay soil, less often (every 7 days). The best irrigation methods for potatoes are drip and sprinkler. Drip irrigation saves water and reduces disease, but it's expensive (US$1,000-2,000 per hectare). Sprinklers are cheaper and common in Africa. For small plots, use watering cans or buckets. A simple setup: a 200-liter drum with a tap and a hose. For larger farms, use a pump and pipes. If you use furrow irrigation, make sure water flows slowly to avoid washing away soil. After planting, irrigate immediately if soil is dry. But if you applied pre-emergence herbicide, wait 24 hours before irrigating to let the chemical settle. Check soil moisture by digging 10 cm deepâif it's dry, irrigate. Too much water causes seed pieces to rot. Too little causes slow sprouting. Once plants emerge, reduce watering slightly to encourage deep roots. In Africa, many farmers rely on rain. If rain is irregular, supplement with irrigation. A rain gauge helps: if you get less than 25 mm per week, irrigate. For drip irrigation, place emitters 20 cm from plant stems. For sprinklers, run them early morning or evening to reduce evaporation. Always monitor for puddlesâif water stands for more than 2 hours, reduce the flow. Proper irrigation can increase yields by 20-30%.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Planting Techniques and Timing for Potato Farming in Africa

Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is one of Africa's fastest-growing food and cash crops, with Kenya, Egypt, South Africa, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Nigeria, and Algeria among the leading producers. For smallholder and emerging commercial farmers alike, the difference between a profitable season and a loss-making one often comes down to decisions made in the first two weeks after seed arrives on the farm: when you plant, how deep you plant, how you space the seed, how you hill and ridge, how you manage weeds before emergence, and how you set up irrigation. This Practical Reference consolidates those decisions into a business-first working document.

Two principles anchor everything below. First, potato is a cool-season crop that produces its best yields when tuber initiation and bulking occur at 15â20Â°C; heat stress above 25Â°C shifts assimilates away from tubers and toward foliage. Second, potato is a high-input, high-return crop â seed, fertilizer, and irrigation costs are substantial, so poor establishment destroys margin faster than almost any other staple. Treat planting as a capital investment, not a routine task.

1. Determining Optimal Planting Dates

In Africa, planting date is dictated by rainfall onset, temperature, and market window rather than by calendar. In the East African highlands (Kenya, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Uganda), the main season is the long rains (MarchâMay) and the short rains (OctoberâDecember). In South Africa's Free State and Limpopo, planting is scheduled so that tuber bulking avoids the hottest months. In Egypt and North Africa, planting runs from late January to mid-February for summer harvest, or AugustâSeptember for winter harvest.

The business rule: plant so that the 60â90 day bulking window falls inside mild temperatures and reliable moisture. Count backwards from your target market delivery date, subtract the variety's maturity class (early 75â90 days, medium 90â110, late 110â130), and subtract a 10â14 day buffer for emergence and establishment.

Table 1. Indicative planting windows for key African potato regions
Region / Country Main planting window Dominant risk Typical variety class
Kenya (Nyandarua, Meru)MarchâApril; OctâNovLate blight, erratic short rainsMedium (90â110 d)
Rwanda & BurundiFebâMarch; SeptâOctBacterial wilt, seed qualityMedium
Ethiopia (Holeta, Bale)AprilâJune (main); SeptFrost at high altitudeMediumâlate
Nigeria (Plateau-Jos)AprilâMay; SeptâOctHeat stress, low seed supplyEarlyâmedium
South Africa (Free State)OctâDec (summer); FebâMar (autumn)Heat, hailEarlyâmedium
Egypt (Nile Delta)JanâFeb; AugâSeptSalinity, heat at bulkingEarly

Source: Compiled from FAO FAOSTAT crop calendars (2023) and CIP regional planting recommendations (2022).

2. Planting Depth and Spacing Guidelines

Depth controls emergence, tuber set, and greening risk. Too shallow (under 5 cm) and tubers green, sunburn, and are exposed to moths; too deep (over 15 cm) and emergence is delayed, seed energy is wasted, and mechanical harvest is difficult. The industry working range is 8â12 cm from the top of the seed piece to the top of the ridge after final hilling.

Spacing determines tuber size profile and marketable yield. Wide spacing â larger tubers (ware/pre-pack). Narrow spacing â more but smaller tubers (seed or processing). Standard commercial spacing in African highlands is 75 cm between rows Ã 25â30 cm in-row, giving roughly 44,000â53,000 plants/ha.

Table 2. Recommended seed spacing by market target
Target market Between rows In-row Plant population Expected tuber size
Ware / fresh market (large)75 cm30â35 cm38,000â44,000/haLarge (80â120 g+)
Seed potato75 cm20â25 cm53,000â66,000/haSmallâmedium (28â45 mm)
Processing (chips/fries)75â90 cm25â30 cm44,000â53,000/haMedium, uniform
Smallholder mixed60â75 cm25â30 cm44,000â55,000/haMixed

Source: Adapted from CIP Potato Seed Production Manual (2020) and KALRO potato agronomy bulletins (2021).

3. Mechanical vs. Manual Planting Methods

Manual planting dominates smallholder systems. Labour is the main cost, but capital outlay is near zero. Typical workflow: open furrow with hoe â place seed â cover â ridge. A trained worker plants 0.1â0.2 ha/day.

Mechanical planting (two-row or four-row planters) suits farms above roughly 20 ha or cooperatives pooling land. Capital cost is high (USD 15,000â60,000 for a tractor-mounted planter), but labour per hectare drops by 60â80%, spacing is uniform, and depth is consistent â all of which translate into higher marketable yield.

Business decision rule: if you cannot keep a planter busy for at least 40â60 ha per year, contract the service rather than buy. In Kenya, Rwanda, and South Africa, custom planting services are increasingly available through cooperatives and machinery rings.

4. Hilling and Ridging After Planting

Hilling (earthing up) is the single most under-rated operation in African potato farming. Done correctly, it:

  • Prevents tuber greening and sunburn;
  • Improves drainage in high-rainfall highlands;
  • Reduces weed competition;
  • Protects tubers from potato tuber moth and late blight spores washing into the soil.

Timing: first hilling when plants are 15â20 cm tall; second hilling 2â3 weeks later, before canopy closure. Final ridge height 20â25 cm, with a broad base to reduce erosion.

5. Use of Pre-Emergence Herbicides

Pre-emergence herbicides are applied to the soil after planting but before potato shoots emerge. They control annual grasses and many broadleaf weeds during the critical first 4â6 weeks, when the crop cannot compete.

Common actives used in African potato systems include metribuzin, pendimethalin, linuron (where registered), and clomazone. Always confirm registration status with your national regulator (e.g., KEPHIS in Kenya, DALRRD in South Africa, NAFDAC in Nigeria).

SAFETY WARNING â Herbicide Handling

Pre-emergence herbicides are hazardous. Always wear nitrile gloves, coveralls, boots, goggles, and a respirator when mixing and spraying. Never mix or spray near drinking water sources, homes, or livestock. Observe the pre-harvest interval and re-entry period on the label. Store pesticides in a locked, labelled cabinet away from food and children. If skin or eye contact occurs, rinse with clean water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Misuse can cause crop failure, groundwater contamination, and serious human poisoning.

6. Irrigation Setup for Newly Planted Potatoes

Potato has a shallow, fibrous root system concentrated in the top 30â40 cm. Newly planted seed needs consistent, light moisture â not flooding. Target 25â30 mm per week during establishment, rising to 35â50 mm/week during tuber bulking.

Recommended systems for African conditions:

  • Drip irrigation â highest water-use efficiency (85â95%), ideal for fertigation, but capital cost USD 1,500â3,000/ha.
  • Sprinkler (solid-set or travelling gun) â moderate cost, suits 2â20 ha farms, but increases late blight risk if run late in the day.
  • Furrow irrigation â low cost but wasteful and uneven; only viable where water is abundant and land is levelled.

Critical rule for newly planted potato: do not over-irrigate before emergence. Saturated soil causes seed piece rot (Erwinia, Pythium) and poor emergence. Irrigate to field capacity, then wait until shoots appear before the next cycle.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm planting window against your region's rainfall onset and target market date â not the calendar.
  2. Use certified seed (min. 28â45 mm for seed class, 45â60 mm for ware) from a registered supplier.
  3. Plant 8â12 cm deep and space 75 Ã 25â30 cm for ware; tighten in-row spacing for seed crops.
  4. Apply pre-emergence herbicide within 48 hours of planting, on moist (not wet) soil, with full PPE.
  5. Hill at 15â20 cm plant height, then again before canopy closure â final ridge 20â25 cm.
  6. Set irrigation to 25â30 mm/week at establishment; avoid waterlogging before emergence.
  7. Scout for late blight from emergence; highland Africa is a permanent blight pressure zone.
  8. Record every input (seed, fertilizer, herbicide, water, labour) â planting decisions only become profitable when measured.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â World Food and Agriculture Statistical Yearbook (latest edition) â crop area, yield and trade data by country.
  • International Potato Center (CIP) â Publications & Technical Manuals â seed systems, agronomy, pest management.
  • Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) â potato variety and agronomy bulletins.
  • South Africa Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD) â potato production guidelines and cultivar lists.
  • International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) â West and Central African crop production resources.

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills Programme â Potato Farming, Module: Planting Techniques and Timing. Always verify input registration and rates with your national regulator before field application.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil temperature range for planting potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Potatoes grow best when soil temperature is between 15Â°C and 20Â°C.

quiz.q: In highland areas of Kenya, when is the main potato planting season?
quiz.explanation: The long rains begin in March to April, making it the main planting season.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to check if soil is ready for planting?
options: A) Squeeze a handful; if it holds together but breaks apart when poked, it's ready.
B) If it drips water, it's ready.
C) If it's bone dry, it's ready.
D) If it's sticky and clumps, it's ready.
quiz.explanation: Soil should be moist but not waterlogged; the squeeze test indicates proper moisture.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid planting potatoes in waterlogged soil?
options: A) It causes seed pieces to rot.
B) It makes tubers turn green.
quiz.explanation: Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen, causing seed pieces to rot.

quiz.q: What is the recommended planting depth for seed potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Planting at 8-10 cm depth balances emergence and protection from greening.

quiz.q: In sandy soils, how deep should you plant potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils dry out faster, so plant deeper to reach moisture.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing between potato rows?
quiz.explanation: 70-90 cm between rows allows air movement and easy hilling.

quiz.q: How many eyes should a cut seed piece have?
quiz.explanation: Each piece needs at least two eyes to sprout and grow.

quiz.q: What should you do after cutting seed potatoes before planting?
options: B) Let them dry in shade for 1-2 days
quiz.explanation: Drying allows the cut surface to heal, reducing rot risk.

quiz.q: How many kilograms of seed potatoes are needed per hectare at 30x75 cm spacing?
quiz.explanation: About 2,000-2,500 kg of seed potatoes are needed per hectare.

quiz.q: Which is a common manual planting tool in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Hand hoes are widely used for manual planting in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a dibber?
options: B) A pointed stick for making holes
quiz.explanation: A dibber is a pointed stick used to make holes for seed pieces.

quiz.q: How many hectares can a person plant manually per day?
quiz.explanation: Manual planting covers about 0.2-0.3 hectares per person per day.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of mechanical planting?
options: B) It requires well-prepared, stone-free soil
C) It cannot plant in rows
D) It uses too much labor
quiz.explanation: Mechanical planters need fine, stone-free soil to work properly.

quiz.q: What is a jab planter?
quiz.explanation: A jab planter is a hand-pushed tool that speeds up manual planting.

quiz.q: When should you first hill potatoes?
options: B) When plants are 5 cm tall
C) When plants are 15-20 cm tall
quiz.explanation: Hilling is done when plants are 15-20 cm tall to cover stems and encourage tuber formation.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of hilling potatoes?
options: B) To prevent tubers from turning green
quiz.explanation: Hilling covers tubers, preventing them from turning green and becoming bitter.

quiz.q: How high should a ridge be when hilling?
quiz.explanation: A ridge of 15-20 cm is ideal for covering stems and tubers.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid hilling when soil is too wet?
options: A) It makes the soil too dry
B) It compacts soil and spreads disease
C) It causes tubers to rot
quiz.explanation: Hilling wet soil compacts it and can spread soil-borne diseases.

quiz.q: How many times do many African farmers hill potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Hilling twiceâfirst at 15 cm and again 2-3 weeks laterâis common practice.

quiz.q: What is a common pre-emergence herbicide for potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Metribuzin (e.g., Sencor) is widely used as a pre-emergence herbicide in potatoes.

quiz.q: When should pre-emergence herbicides be applied?
quiz.explanation: Pre-emergence herbicides must be applied before potato plants emerge.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of metribuzin 70% WP per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Apply 0.5-1.0 kg of metribuzin 70% WP per hectare.

quiz.q: Why should you not spray pre-emergence herbicide if rain is expected within 6 hours?
options: A) Rain washes the herbicide away
B) Rain makes the herbicide toxic
C) Rain activates the herbicide too fast
D) Rain causes weeds to grow
quiz.explanation: Rain can wash the herbicide off the soil before it forms a barrier.

quiz.q: What should you do if weeds have already emerged before applying pre-emergence herbicide?
quiz.explanation: Pre-emergence herbicides only work on weed seeds, not emerged weeds.

quiz.q: What is a safe alternative to herbicides for organic farmers?
quiz.explanation: Mulch suppresses weeds without chemicals.

quiz.q: How much water per week do newly planted potatoes need?
quiz.explanation: Apply about 20-25 mm of water per week for consistent moisture.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method saves the most water?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots, minimizing waste.

quiz.q: After applying pre-emergence herbicide, how long should you wait before irrigating?
quiz.explanation: Wait 24 hours to let the herbicide settle and form a barrier.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to measure rainfall for irrigation decisions?
quiz.explanation: A rain gauge helps you know if you need to supplement with irrigation.
